headline: A rough day across the board — the ASX fell 1.6% and US markets took a heavy hit last night, while GTA 6's $3.8bn launch day is the standout story for TTWO holders.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: Biggest mover today. The AI trade is under pressure — Wall Street analysts are openly questioning whether the AI investment boom has legs, and that sentiment dragged AI-focused ETFs down hard. Down 4% today and sitting 21.6% below your cost basis overall. The long-term AI thesis is still intact, but this is a volatile sector.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: A rare bright spot — PLS bounced 2.3% today. That said, the broader lithium story remains challenging, with reports flagging rising Chinese supply and a potential 2027 oversupply. Today's gain is a small relief rally rather than a turning point.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Fell 2.4% today, dragged lower by global risk-off sentiment (investors moving away from riskier assets). Emerging markets tend to get hit hardest when global confidence dips. No specific bad news — this is broader market turbulence.

movers.name: DHHF (BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF)
movers.note: Down 2.3% today, reflecting the broad ASX and global selloff. DHHF holds a wide basket of global shares, so when markets fall across the board, it follows. Nothing structural to worry about here.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: Fell 2.8% today on the ASX, tracking the sharp US market drop from last night — the NASDAQ fell over 5% and the S&P 500 dropped 3.7%. VTS mirrors the entire US share market, so it moves in lockstep.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: Down 2.1% today. VDHG holds a mix of Aussie and global shares, so the broad selloff on both the ASX and US markets dragged it lower. No fund-specific issues — pure market noise.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dropped 2.8% last night in the US selloff. Some commentary is questioning whether MSFT's valuation (still above Alphabet's) is justified given its AI spending. Despite the dip, your position is still up 9.4% overall — the long-term story hasn't changed.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: GOOG slid 2.6% last night. Alphabet is down nearly 20% from recent highs, with one analyst flagging concerns about its $9.1 billion cash burn rate. That said, some analysts see this as a potential buying opportunity, noting the stock looks oversold. Your position is down 14.1% overall.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO edged up 0.65% last night — a relatively calm session considering the bombshell news: GTA 6 launched and raked in $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales, the biggest entertainment launch in history. The market had largely priced in a blockbuster launch; expect more movement as the full sales picture emerges.

watch_today.title: GTA 6 smashes records — TTWO is the story of the week
watch_today.detail: GTA 6 pulled in $3.79 billion on day one — the biggest entertainment launch ever, beating every film, album, or game before it. Take-Two's stock only moved 0.65% last night, suggesting the market had partly priced this in, but the sales momentum over the coming weeks could drive further upside. For a long-term holder, this is a very good sign. Hold and watch the trajectory.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX taking a beating — but is the AI trade really over?
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF is down 4% today and 21.6% from what you paid. Wall Street analysts are starting to publicly question whether the AI spending boom can sustain. This is a real risk to watch, but the multi-year AI buildout story isn't dead — it's just volatile. For a long-term holder, this is uncomfortable but not a reason to bail. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: GOOG down nearly 20% from highs — long-term case still intact
watch_today.detail: Alphabet has had a rough run, dropping 2.6% last night and sitting well below recent highs. One analyst is flagging $9.1bn in cash burn as a concern, but others see the stock as genuinely oversold and a potential buy. Your position is small (under $100 value). The long-term case for Google — search dominance, cloud growth, AI integration — hasn't changed. Hold.

watch_today.title: RBA rate cuts coming — good news for your Aussie holdings
watch_today.detail: Australia's unemployment rate has jumped to 4.9%, a five-year high, and NAB has already cut home loan rates in response. Markets are now pricing in RBA rate cuts (the Reserve Bank lowering official interest rates). Lower rates are generally good for share prices, especially ETFs like VDHG and DHHF. Keep an eye on the next RBA meeting.

watch_today.title: PLS bounced today — but the lithium outlook remains cloudy
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals is up 2.3% today, a welcome relief. But reports out today warn that rising Chinese lithium supply and a looming 2027 oversupply could keep prices suppressed. PLS is already down 61% from your cost — the thesis here needs a lithium price recovery to play out. Hold for now, no new buying case yet.

watch_today.title: Broad market selloff — don't panic, this is long-term noise
watch_today.detail: Last night the NASDAQ fell 5.3% and the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% — a sharp, painful session. Today the ASX followed down 1.6%. Your whole portfolio is red today. For a long-term buy-and-hold investor, single-day selloffs like this are normal turbulence. Nothing in your holdings has fundamentally changed overnight. Stay the course.

world.summary: GTA 6 makes history, tensions simmer over Iran, the Middle East war continues, and global markets face a 'two-speed' economic outlook.

stories.title: GTA 6 launches to $3.8 billion in a single day — the biggest entertainment event in history
stories.why_it_matters: Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI launched and immediately shattered every entertainment sales record ever set, pulling in $3.79 billion USD on its very first day. That's more than any movie opening weekend, any concert tour, any album launch — ever. The game was 13 years in the making. For context, the previous record holder (GTA 5) earned about $1 billion in its first three days back in 2013. This is a genuine cultural and economic milestone — and directly relevant if you hold Take-Two stock (TTWO), Rockstar's parent company.

stories.title: Trump says Iran may be developing chemical or biological weapons as tensions rise
stories.why_it_matters: President Trump has publicly accused Tehran of potentially working on chemical or biological weapons, ratcheting up rhetoric against Iran at a time when Middle East tensions are already elevated. This kind of accusation from a sitting US president raises the risk of military escalation in the region. If conflict with Iran intensifies, oil prices — currently at $84/barrel — could spike sharply, which would flow through to Australian petrol prices and global inflation.

stories.title: Middle East war: Israeli opposition figure Eisenkot signals willingness to lead emergency government
stories.why_it_matters: Israeli opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot has said he's ready to lead an emergency government as prime minister, without a rotation deal with Benjamin Netanyahu. This signals growing political pressure inside Israel, where the ongoing war is creating fault lines in the governing coalition. A change in Israeli leadership could shift the direction of the conflict — and any ceasefire or escalation affects the entire Middle East region, including oil supply and global market confidence.

stories.title: Trump's DOJ backs away from election fraud cases and Alaska Senate challenge
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration's Department of Justice has moved to drop its legal challenge to Democrat Mary Peltola's Alaska Senate election win, and is more broadly pulling back from election fraud cases. This follows a pattern of the Trump DOJ unwinding legal actions related to the 2024 and 2026 elections. Critics say it represents the politicisation of federal law enforcement; supporters see it as cutting unnecessary litigation. Either way, it reshapes the political landscape heading into the next electoral cycle.

stories.title: Global economy at risk of splitting into a 'two-speed world' — developed vs developing nations
stories.why_it_matters: Economic analysts are warning that the global economy is at risk of splitting into a 'two-speed world' — where wealthy, developed nations (US, Europe, Australia) recover and grow, while developing economies fall further behind. This matters for Australian investors because a large chunk of ETFs like VGE (Vanguard Emerging Markets) are exposed to developing economies. If this divergence deepens, emerging market returns could lag significantly.

markets.summary: A brutal night on Wall Street — the NASDAQ cratered 5.3% and the S&P 500 shed 3.7%, dragging the ASX down 1.6% today. Gold sold off sharply, the Aussie dollar dipped, and oil ticked up slightly.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: The local market followed Wall Street's lead and fell 1.6% today, closing at 8,593.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session saw the S&P 500 drop 3.7% — a significant one-day fall. Broad risk-off selling hit US markets hard.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: The tech-heavy NASDAQ fell 5.3% last night — the biggest drop of the major indices. AI and tech stocks bore the brunt of the selloff.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil edged up slightly to $84/barrel, with Middle East tension providing some upward pressure despite the broader market selloff.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold fell sharply by 4.6% — unusual, since gold usually rises when markets fall. This may reflect investors selling gold to cover losses elsewhere (a 'margin call' effect).

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar slipped slightly to US$0.662. With unemployment rising and RBA rate cuts expected, the AUD may remain under pressure in the near term.

politics.summary: Australia's unemployment rate hits a five-year high at 4.9%, firing up the RBA rate cut debate. Labor faces scrutiny over internet censorship laws, housing policy misfires, and rising government spending. Meanwhile, Xi Jinping praises the Australia-China reset.

stories.title: Unemployment hits 4.9% — a five-year high — and NAB cuts mortgage rates in response
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's unemployment rate has surged to 4.9%, the highest in five years, catching economists off guard. NAB moved quickly to cut its home loan rates in response, and markets are now pricing in RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) rate cuts sooner than expected. Lower interest rates would be good news for mortgage holders and would typically boost share prices. A recession debate is now openly starting, with some analysts calling it a 'pretty clear' signal the RBA's tightening cycle is done.

stories.title: Xi Jinping says Australia-China relations have made a 'full turnaround', praises Albanese
stories.why_it_matters: Chinese President Xi Jinping has publicly praised PM Anthony Albanese, saying the two countries have achieved a 'full turnaround' in their relationship after years of trade tensions and diplomatic friction. This is significant for Australia's economy — China is our biggest trading partner, buying much of our iron ore, coal, and agricultural exports. A warmer relationship means fewer trade barriers and greater stability for Australian exporters.

stories.title: Labor's proposed internet laws spark censorship fears
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government is pushing new internet regulation laws that critics say could restrict free speech and lead to censorship of online content. Civil liberties groups and media organisations are raising alarms that the laws give authorities too much power to control what Australians can say and see online. The government says the laws are aimed at harmful misinformation, but the debate over where the line sits is intensifying.

stories.title: Housing policies backfiring as buyers retreat and rental crisis worsens
stories.why_it_matters: New analysis shows government housing policies are producing the opposite effect to what was intended — first home buyers are retreating from the market rather than entering it, while the rental crisis continues to worsen. Renters are being squeezed by high rents, while would-be buyers say incentives aren't enough to offset high prices and mortgage costs. With unemployment now rising, housing affordability is set to become a bigger political flashpoint heading toward the next election.

stories.title: Chalmers under pressure as federal spending hits 40% of GDP
stories.why_it_matters: The AFR is reporting that federal government spending has hit 40% of GDP — a level last seen during the COVID emergency — putting pressure on Treasurer Jim Chalmers to rein in expenditure. Critics argue the high spending is adding to inflationary pressure and limiting the RBA's ability to cut rates. Chalmers is reportedly beginning to use the word 'cuts' (in spending), signalling a possible fiscal tightening ahead.

ai.summary: The AI investment trade is under scrutiny as Wall Street questions its sustainability, while governments in New York and the US Senate move to regulate AI more aggressively. The public mood toward Big Tech is souring.

stories.title: Wall Street forecasters are starting to wonder if the AI trade is running out of steam
stories.why_it_matters: Some of Wall Street's most prominent forecasters are publicly flagging concerns that the AI investment boom — which has driven massive gains in tech stocks over the past two years — may be approaching its limits. The worry is that companies have spent enormous sums on AI infrastructure without yet proving the returns justify the cost. This is directly relevant to your GXAI.AX holding, which is an ETF that bets on AI companies. The ETF is down 21.6% from your purchase price, and this sentiment is part of why.

stories.title: New York creates a dedicated AI enforcement unit to police how AI is used
stories.why_it_matters: New York State has launched a dedicated AI enforcement unit — a team of regulators specifically tasked with policing how artificial intelligence is used in business and government. This follows a broader trend of US states stepping in to regulate AI while federal rules remain patchy. For AI companies (and ETFs that hold them), more regulation means more compliance costs and potential restrictions on how products can be built or deployed.

stories.title: US Senate Democrats push to establish a select committee on AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: Democratic senators are pushing to create a dedicated Senate committee focused specifically on regulating artificial intelligence, wanting to move quickly before the technology outpaces the law. This is a significant moment — a select committee would have real power to shape AI laws covering everything from privacy and bias to national security. For tech companies and AI investors, the direction of US federal AI rules will matter enormously in the years ahead.

stories.title: Public mood toward Big Tech has shifted — and it may not be coming back
stories.why_it_matters: A new analysis argues that America's relationship with Big Tech has fundamentally changed — the 'vibes' that once made companies like Google, Meta, and Amazon culturally beloved have shifted to suspicion and resentment. This matters for investors because public sentiment affects regulation, advertising revenue, and hiring. Companies like Alphabet and Microsoft aren't just fighting business battles now — they're fighting a trust deficit that could take years to repair.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — Roosters 19, Knights 18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. The 2027 season draw is out, the AFL Draft wrapped up with Port Adelaide landing the top pick, and GTA 6's launch is the crossover story of the week.

stories.title: Roosters pip Knights 19-18 in NRL Grand Final thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters have won the 2026 NRL premiership, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in a one-point Grand Final at Accor Stadium. It was as close as it gets — Knights fans will be absolutely heartbroken. The Roosters take their place in the history books with another title.

stories.title: 2027 NRL draw released — Tigers cop a brutal early run, Grand Finalists start tough
stories.why_it_matters: The 2027 NRL draw has dropped and analysts are already calling winners and losers. The Wests Tigers have copped a brutal early schedule, while the Grand Finalists — Roosters and Knights — face tough starts to 2027. The draw also confirms a Canberra Raiders match in Wagga Wagga in May 2027, the first NRL game in the regional city.

stories.title: NRL players say season is too long; NRLW players say theirs is too short
stories.why_it_matters: A player poll released today shows NRL players feel the men's season is too long and physically draining, while NRLW (women's) players feel their competition is too short and want more games. The findings are likely to put pressure on the NRL to rethink the season structure — particularly for the men's competition, which has expanded significantly in recent years.

stories.title: Port Adelaide snags AFL's top 2026 draft pick
stories.why_it_matters: Port Adelaide has secured the number one pick in the 2026 AFL Draft, landing the most coveted young player in this year's crop. The Power had a disappointing season and will be hoping the top pick can accelerate their rebuild. The AFL Draft night also featured a wild story involving a new Bulldogs player's celebration party and chaos around the Cats' bids.
